2006B16.goal: Feb 29, 2004 was a Sunday; we want the weekday of Feb 29, 2020. Count days between them mod $7$.

tools.name: Days in a year
tools.why: Each ordinary year shifts the weekday by $1$.

check.q: What day is $6$ days after Sunday?
check.why: One day before the next Sunday.

2006B16.shortcut: Each leap-to-leap span of $4$ years shifts by $5$: $4\cdot5=20\equiv6$.
2006B16.recognize: Day-of-week jumps: days mod $7$, with $365\equiv1$ and $366\equiv2$.

2006B17.goal: Alice moves a random ball to Bob; Bob returns a random ball from his $6$. We want $P(\text{bags end the same})$. That happens exactly when Bob returns a ball of the colour Alice sent.

tools.name: Conditioning
tools.why: By symmetry any colour behaves the same.

tools.name: Counting matches
tools.why: Bob's original plus the one Alice sent.

2006B17.approach: After Alice's move, Bob has $6$ balls, $2$ of the colour she sent. He must return one of those: $\tfrac26=\tfrac13$.

steps.title: Condition
steps.explain: The bags match iff Bob sends back the same colour Alice gave.

check.q: How many balls of Alice's colour does Bob have after her move?

2006B17.bridge: Bob must return the duplicated colour.
solution: Bob has $6$ balls with $2$ of Alice's colour.
2006B17.shortcut: Alice's choice doesn't matter: only Bob's single draw does.
2006B17.recognize: Exchange problems: condition on the first move and count what restores the original state.

2006B18.goal: $a_1=2$, $a_2=3$, $a_n=\tfrac{a_{n-1}}{a_{n-2}}$. We want $a_{2006}$. Compute terms until they repeat.

tools.name: Periodicity
tools.fact: \text{the recursion depends on two terms; a repeated pair repeats forever}

2006B18.bridge: Find the period, reduce the index.
2006B18.recognize: Recurrences with division: usually periodic — compute until a pair repeats.

2006B19.goal: Unit square $OABC$ at the centre of a radius-$2$ circle; $AB$ and $CB$ extended past $B$ hit the circle at $D$ and $E$. We want the area between $BD$, $BE$ and the arc $DE$. Use coordinates: it's a sector minus two triangles.
2006B19.approach: Region $=$ sector $DOE$ minus triangles $ODB$ and $OBE$. Sector $=\tfrac{30}{360}\cdot4\pi=\tfrac\pi3$. Each triangle has area $\tfrac{\sqrt3-1}{2}$.

check.q: What angle does $(1,\sqrt3)$ make with the $x$-axis?

steps.title: Triangles
steps.explain: $\triangle ODB$: base $BD=\sqrt3-1$ on $x=1$, height $1$: area $\tfrac{\sqrt3-1}2$. Same for $\triangle OBE$. Region $=\tfrac\pi3-(\sqrt3-1)$.

2006B19.shortcut: Sanity: the region is small, $\approx0.315$, matching (A).
2006B19.recognize: Region between two segments and an arc: sector minus the polygon joining the centre.

2006B20.goal: Rectangle with $A=(6,-22)$, $B=(2006,178)$, $D=(8,y)$. We want the area. $AD\perp AB$ fixes $y$.
2006B20.bridge: Dot product gives $y$; multiply the side lengths.
2006B20.recognize: Rectangles from coordinates: perpendicularity via the dot product.

2006B21.goal: Each die shows $k$ with probability $\tfrac{k}{21}$. We want $P(\text{total }7)$. Sum over the six pairs $(k,7-k)$.
2006B21.bridge: Weight each pair by the product of probabilities.
2006B21.shortcut: Pairs come in equal mirror pairs: $2(6+10+12)=56$.
2006B21.recognize: Weighted dice: write $P(k)$ explicitly and sum products.

2006B22.goal: $N$ sandwiches, each with $B$ globs ($4$¢) and $J$ blobs ($5$¢), cost $253$¢ total. With $N>1$ and all positive integers, we want the jam cost $5NJ$. Factor $253$.

steps.title: Find $N$
steps.explain: $4B+5J=11$ has no positive solutions ($9$ is the minimum, next values $13,14,\ldots$). So $N=11$.

2006B22.bridge: Factor the total; test the per-sandwich cost.
2006B22.shortcut: $4B+5J=23$: $J$ must be odd ($23-5J$ divisible by $4$), so $J=3$.
traps: Answering the total or peanut-butter cost.
2006B22.recognize: Integer totals with a product structure: factor the total.

2006B23.goal: Two cevians $BE$ and $CF$ meet at $P$; $[PFB]=3$, $[PBC]=7$, $[PCE]=7$, and quadrilateral $AFPE$ is unknown. Draw $AP$ to split it into $x=[AFP]$ and $y=[APE]$, then use ratios along each side.

tools.name: Ratio along a side
tools.why: Triangles with the same apex and bases on $AB$.

2006B23.approach: $\tfrac x3=\tfrac{x+y+7}{10}$ and $\tfrac y7=\tfrac{x+y+3}{14}$. Solve the linear system.
2006B23.bridge: Split by $AP$ and write two ratio equations.
traps: Assuming the quadrilateral equals the sum of the triangles.
Using a ratio with the wrong pair of triangles.
2006B23.recognize: Cevian area puzzles: draw the third segment from the vertex to the intersection and set up ratios.

2006B24.goal: Externally tangent circles ($r=2$ at $O$, $R=4$ at $P$, $OP=6$) with common external tangents $AD$ and $BC$. We want the area of hexagon $AOBCPD$. It is two congruent right trapezoids $AOPD$ and $BOPC$.
2006B24.bridge: Split along $OP$ into two right trapezoids.
2006B24.shortcut: Tangent length between circles: external uses $R-r$, internal uses $R+r$.
2006B24.recognize: Shapes made from radii and tangents: right trapezoids.

2006B25.goal: A $4$-digit number with two digits each appearing twice is divisible by all eight children's ages. The oldest is $9$, so the ages are $1$–$9$ with exactly one of $1$–$8$ missing. We want the age that is not there. Test whether $5$ can be an age.

tools.name: Evenness is forced
tools.fact: \text{at least one of }4,6,8\text{ is an age}
tools.why: Only one age from $1$–$8$ is missing.

2006B25.approach: If $5$ were an age, the number (even) would end in $0$, so its digits are $0$ and $9$. The father's age is the last two digits, so the number is $9090$, which fails $4$ and $8$ — two missing ages. So $5$ is missing; check with $5544=2^3\cdot3^2\cdot7\cdot11$.

steps.title: Rule out 5
steps.explain: Even and divisible by $5$ means it ends in $0$. With $a+b=9$ the digits are $0,9$; ending in $90$ gives $9090$, not divisible by $4$ or $8$.

check.q: Why must the number be even?

steps.title: Confirm
steps.explain: $5544=8\cdot693=8\cdot9\cdot7\cdot11$ is divisible by $1,2,3,4,6,7,8,9$ but not $5$; father is $44$.

2006B25.bridge: Show $5$ forces a contradiction, then exhibit a working plate.
solution: The number is even (some of $4,6,8$ are ages).
If $5$ divided it, it would be $9090$, which fails $4$ and $8$.
So $5$ is not an age; $5544$ works.
2006B25.shortcut: $5$ and $2$ together force a final $0$, which is very restrictive.
traps: Trying to find the plate by brute force without the digit-sum rule.
Forgetting the father's age must be a sensible two-digit number.
2006B25.recognize: "Divisible by all but one of $1$–$9$": check which single divisor causes a contradiction.
